newsitem.title: USA: N.Y. sues tobacco companies, had talks with industry.
newsitem.headline: N.Y. sues tobacco companies, had talks with industry.

text.p: By Gail Appleson, Law Correspondent

New York became a major player in the fight against the tobacco industry Monday when it sued the industry to recoup health care costs of smokers and sought the dissolution of two industry affiliated groups.

New York Attorney General Dennis Vacco also revealed he had proposed last year that the industry pay the state $656 million to head off the lawsuit and said cigarette makers responded with a "laughable" counteroffer of less than $5 million.
Lucia Valente, chief special counsel to Vacco, told Reuters that she believed New York was the first state to offer a proposal directly to the tobacco industry.

Anti-smoking forces were elated by the filing of the suit because New York has the largest Medicaid population of any of the plaintiffs that have filed this type of suit so far. They also were surprised because they doubted that Vacco would join in their battle.
Some $2.6 billion is spent annually by private insurance companies and the Medicaid programme to treat smoking-related illness in New York.

"New York is the biggest player yet. We were not expecting it to join in ... this gives the Medicaid litigation a tremendous boost," said Richard Daynard who heads the Tobacco Product Liability Project at Northeastern Law School.

"What's extraordinary is that Vacco, who is known as a conservative Republican, has showed little to no sign that he would seriously consider suing the industry," said Daynard, an anti-smoking proponent who tracks tobacco litigation.

The defendants named in the lawsuit include R.J. Reynolds Tobacco, a division of RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp.; Philip Morris Cos. Inc.; Brown and Williamson Tobacco Corp., which is owned by B.A.T Industries Plc; Loews Corp.'s Lorillard Tobacco Co.; and Brooke Group Ltd.'s Liggett Group Inc.
Philip Morris, Brown & Williamson and R.J. Reynolds Tobacco all denied having settlement talks with Vacco's office and said his suit was without merit.
Reynolds spokeswoman Peggy Carter said while company officials had met with Vacco's staff to explain why they thought his suit would fail, there was no discussion of any proposals involving money.
"We've had no conversations like this," she said.

Vacco is the the 19th state attorney general to sue the tobacco industry to recoup Medicaid health care costs of smokers. Alabama's lieutentant governor also filed a private lawsuit against the industry, and Alaska recently said it was seriously considering a lawsuit.
New York City and the California cities of San Francisco and San Jose and Los Angeles County also have sued.

If New York State should prevail in its lawsuit, Vacco said the damages could be in the billions of dollars, making New York's earlier offer "seem like pocket change." The lawsuit, filed in state court in Manhattan, seeks unspecified damages.

The 120-page complaint accuses the companies of racketeering by hiding health information, manipulating nicotine content, derailing the development of safer cigarettes and marketing tobacco products to minors.

Vacco said while other states had sued the industry's research groups -- the Washington-based Tobacco Institute and the New York-based Council for Tobacco Research USA Inc. -- the New York lawsuit is the first to seek their dissolution. He said this action was possible under state laws governing non-profit agencies. The Tobacco Institute said it would not comment on litigation.
Vacco said while the two groups were supposed to conduct impartial studies of the effects of tobacco, they were merely a "front for publicity" by misleading the public.
The filing of the lawsuit comes as Brooke Group Ltd. Chairman Bennett LeBow is seeking a settlement with all states that have filed Medicaid lawsuits against tobacco makers.

Brooke is the parent of Liggett Group Inc., the first tobacco company to ever settle cigarette lawsuits. It shocked the financial community in March 1996 when it reached an accord with five states that sued the industry to recoup health care costs of smokers.

The lawsuit also comes when some state attorneys general and some plaintiffs lawyers also are seeking a possible legislative solution to the mounting litigation against the tobacco industry. The group has been meeting with intermediaries with contacts in the tobacco industry. Cigarette companies deny any participation in the talks.
Vacco, however, said he did not file the lawsuit to try to get in on any of these settlement talks and that litigation may be the only answer.
Special Counsel Valente, who was on the state's negotiating team, said in an interview, "They had an attitude ... that they can't be beaten."
